q: Across the three walk-forward folds, is FOODS_1's forecast value add improving or deteriorating?
answer: Improving, monotonically across the three folds — though it only turns positive in the final fold. FOODS_1 FVA: fold 1 (2013-05-05 to 2013-07-26) -16.3 pp, fold 2 (2013-07-27 to 2013-10-24) -8.4 pp, fold 3 (2013-10-25 to 2014-01-22) +4.3 pp. Caveat on the driver: model accuracy itself is not steadily rising (71.5% -> 77.5% -> 75.9%); the fold-3 flip comes largely from the naive baseline degrading (87.8% -> 85.9% -> 71.6%) in the holiday-period window. Over the full 263-day backtest FOODS_1 still lands at -7.3 pp FVA, i.e. it does not beat the seasonal-naive baseline overall.

q: What was FOODS_3's single worst forecast day, and would the naive baseline have done better on that day?
answer: FOODS_3's worst day was Christmas Day, 2013-12-25, when the store sold 0 units but the model predicted 2,431.5  o,5 units of absolute error. q: FOODS_1 loses to the naive baseline over the whole backtest — was that also true in December 2013?
answer: No — the sign flips in December 2013. Over the full 263-day backtest FOODS_1 is the clear loser to the baseline: 75.0% forecast accuracy vs 82.2% naive, FVA -7.3pp. But in the window 2013-12-01 to 2013-12-31 the model beat the baseline by +10.2pp (72.0% vs 61.8%). Note this is not because the model got better — its December accuracy (72.0%) is below its own full-backtest 75.0%. It is because the naive baseline collapsed over the holidays: repeating last week's same weekday breaks down around Christmas. The clearest case is 2013-12-25, when actual units were 0; the naive error was 436.0 units against the model's 298.6 units. The model still had bad holiday days of its own (2013-12-21: actual 625, model 298.6, error 326.4 units vs naive 182.0). Scope: FOODS_1 only, calendar December 2013, accuracy measured the same way as the headline figures.

q: Does FOODS_1 ever beat the naive baseline in any single backtest fold?

Over the full 263-day backtest FOODS_1 still trails: FA 75.0% vs naive 82.2%, FVA -7.3pp.

q: Is the model getting better over time?

output.note: volume_units is total units sold over the 263-day backtest window

answer: No — if anything it is drifting worse, and it never beats the naive baseline. Pooled over the 263 days the model is at 79.5% accuracy vs 85.2% for seasonal-naive (FVA -5.7pp), with only 2 of 7 departments beating naive. Across the three sequential walk-forward folds the two largest departments both degrade: FOODS_3 goes 81.8% -> 80.4% -> 78.2% (naive 87.8 / 88.1 / 85.3; FVA -6.0 -> -7.7 -> -7.1pp), and HOUSEHOLD_1 goes 83.8% -> 77.3% -> 73.6% (naive 88.8 / 88.4 / 85.9; FVA -5.0 -> -11.1 -> -12.3pp). The weekly trend agrees: early weeks run in the low-to-mid 80s (e.g. 86.4% week of 2013-05-20), while the last three weeks are 79.9%, 76.0% and 68.8% against naive 83.6%, 87.4% and 89.9%. The only weeks the model clearly leads are the holiday-disruption weeks when naive collapses (week of 2013-12-02: model 83.0% vs naive 72.7%; week of 2013-12-30: 84.1% vs 73.9%). Scope: pooled weekly trend plus fold-level detail for the two highest-volume departments.

q: What caused the spike in FOODS_1 sales on December 21st 2013?

output.note: volume_units is total units sold over the 263-day backtest window

answer: I can't tell you the cause — the backtest holds only actual/model/naive unit series, with no promotion, price, event or holiday-driver fields, so nothing in the data attributes the spike to a reason. What I can confirm is the spike itself and that it sits in a multi-day pre-Christmas run-up: FOODS_1 sold 625 units on 2013-12-21, the department's largest error day (model 298.6, naive 443.0, absolute error 326.4). It was the peak of a rising stretch — 465 units on 12-20, 625 on 12-21, 571 on 12-22, 535 on 12-23, 486 on 12-24 — followed by a zero-sales day on 2013-12-25 (store closed) and 179 units on 12-26. The model held flat at 298.6 units throughout and missed the whole run-up, but any causal explanation (holiday stock-up, promotion, etc.) would be inference beyond what these tools return.
